statement: In adults who smoked, mostly moderately to heavily, and stopped (12 placebo-controlled trials published from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each; a systematic review without pooling, funded by SmithKline Beecham; West & Shiffman, 2001), using nicotine gum (8 trials), a nicotine inhaler (3) or a sublingual nicotine tablet (1) compared with a placebo product is associated with fewer withdrawal symptoms in the first week after stopping: irritability was lower in all 9 trials that reported it, total withdrawal discomfort in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4 and low mood in the only trial that reported it, while results were mixed for restlessness (2 of 5), poor concentration (5 of 9), sleep disturbance (1 of 2) and hunger (2 of 5). Craving was lower in 7 of 11 trials: in all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet but in only 3 of the 7 gum trials. The review counted significant results and gives no sizes; where a trial did not report a symptom the table is blank, so non-significant results may be missing. Five trials kept people who had smoked again in their analyses, more people dropped out of the placebo groups in three, and one trial used low-nicotine gum as its comparator. No trial of the lozenge was found, nothing is known beyond the first week, and patches and nasal spray were not included. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In 12 older studies, people who had just stopped smoking were less irritable in the first week if they used nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet than if they used a dummy product without nicotine. Most studies also found less overall discomfort and anxiety. Cravings were lower in all the inhaler and tablet studies but in fewer than half of the gum studies. The review only counted which studies found a difference, not how big it was, and a medicine company (SmithKline Beecham) paid for it.
population: Adults who smoked (mostly moderate to heavy smoking), without psychiatric or acute physical illness, who stopped in placebo-controlled trials published 1984 to 2000
exposure: Oral nicotine products: nicotine gum, inhaler or sublingual tablet (study conditions in the study card)
comparator: A placebo product of the same kind (low-nicotine gum in one trial)
outcome: Withdrawal symptoms and craving in the first week of abstinence, counted as significant or not in each trial
magnitude: No effect sizes. Fractions of trials with a significant reduction: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1), poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, hunger 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Materials and methods › Search strategy; Selection and characterisation of studies; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of 27 studies reporting effects of oral nicotine on at least one withdrawal symptom, 12 met the criteria (published placebo-controlled randomized trials, product started within 24 hours of stopping, symptoms assessed over at least 24 hours in the usual environment, biochemical verification): 8 gum, 3 inhaler, 1 sublingual tablet and no lozenge; good data existed only for the first week.

evidence.locator: Table 3, bottom row and n column (read on the rendered, rotated page)
evidence.extracted: Fractions of trials finding a significant effect in the first week: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2, hunger 2/5, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11; trials had 15 to 240 participants.
Craving was reduced in all three inhaler trials and the single tablet trial but in only 3 of 7 gum trials.

Lapsers were kept in the analyses in five trials (Hughes et al., 1984, 1989, 1990 and 1991; Gross & Stitzer, 1989); more people dropped out of the placebo group in three trials; West et al. (1984) used low-nicotine gum rather than placebo as the comparator.

The authors state that in most trials people were analysed even if only partially abstinent, and that the number of studies was too small for any pattern to show unless very marked; no differences were seen by date, size, inclusion of lapsers, use of baselines or product use.
Blanks in Table 3 mean that the effect was not tested or not reported; the review was funded by SmithKline Beecham.

risk_of_bias.note: Five trials kept people who smoked again in the analyses, attrition was high and sometimes unequal, one comparator contained nicotine, and blinding was not assessed.

inconsistency.note: Irritability and total discomfort are consistent; the mixed symptoms are reported as mixed.

indirectness.note: Worded for the products, people and first week studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the statement says sizes are unknown.

publication_bias.note: Counts of significant results in published trials, with blanks that may hide unreported null results, in a manufacturer-funded review.

grade.reasoning: Randomized placebo-controlled trials start high. Risk of bias −1 and publication or reporting bias −1 give low. The claim gives directions only; the size of any reduction is unknown. Status replicated: all nine trials that reported irritability, from several groups, agree, as do six of seven for total withdrawal; craving with gum is not replicated (3 of 7).
